messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 35
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Special Education Teacher
  trauma_type: Mugging or robbery
  pcl5: 58

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Shouting: Shouting, Somatic Pain (Neck): Neck pain, Authority Presence: Police
  Threat: Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
  Memory: Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind., Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Inadequacy: I am inadequate

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Daniel Weber, a 35-year-old special education teacher, traced the start of his difficulties to an evening mugging eight months earlier. He had stayed late at school preparing individualized lesson materials and left carrying a backpack full of student files. On the walk to his car, a man came up behind him, shouted at him to hand everything over, and yanked him by the shoulder hard enough to wrench his neck. Daniel remembered seeing, almost frame by frame, the man’s mouth open in a yell, the angle of the parking lot lights, the pressure in his neck, and then the sudden arrival of police lights after it was over. What stayed with him most was not only fear but a hot, humiliating rage that he had been overpowered so quickly, mixed with guilt that he had been carrying school materials and had, in his mind, “put himself in that position” by leaving alone so late.

In the weeks that followed, those details did not soften. Daniel described the memory as if he were looking at still photographs laid out in front of him rather than remembering something finished and past. Certain moments in daily life pulled those images up immediately. If a student raised his voice sharply in the classroom, or if shouting echoed in the hallway, he was back in the parking lot for a second, seeing the mugger’s face and feeling the surge of rage and guilt that came with it. Neck pain was especially potent; if he turned too fast while helping a child and felt a twinge, the image of being grabbed returned with startling clarity. The sight of police near school dismissal could do the same. Even though he knew they were there for ordinary reasons, their presence called up the aftermath of the robbery so vividly that he would momentarily feel as if the event were happening again.

As Daniel tried to make sense of what had happened, he had come to believe it said something basic and damning about him. Somebody else, he thought, would not have gotten into this situation. A more capable man would have noticed danger earlier, reacted faster, fought back better. He spoke about himself as inadequate in a flat, convinced way. From that position, being constantly on guard felt necessary rather than excessive. He was certain he had to monitor everything because he was the kind of person things happened to. Even in safe places he could not relax; the conviction that he was vulnerable and insufficient kept his body braced, his attention fixed on possible threat, and his eyes moving automatically to exits the moment he entered any room or building.

Those same harsh conclusions also colored the way he remembered the mugging. When the scene came back to him, it did not come as a neutral replay. It arrived with self-accusation already attached: he saw the images and immediately judged himself against an imagined other person who would have handled it differently. The more inadequate he felt, the more guilt there was in the remembering, and the more the memory burned with rage at the mugger and at himself.

By the time he sought treatment, the sense of current danger and the memories were feeding each other tightly. Because he was so keyed up, any loud voice at school, any pull in his neck, any glimpse of a police officer in the parking lot was noticed instantly and felt loaded. That constant monitoring made the world seem full of reminders, and the reminders brought back the photographic flashes of the attack. Once that happened, he would feel himself jolt into the same state again—heart racing, body tight, unable to settle, scanning the classroom door and nearby exits as though he might need to move his students to safety. He hated that he sometimes became less available to the children when this happened; while a child was dysregulated and shouting, part of Daniel was managing the lesson and part of him was no longer fully in the room.

Over months, this pattern deepened his view of himself. Each episode in which he froze internally or stayed tense for hours afterward seemed to prove that he was inadequate and that other people would cope better. That belief, in turn, kept him watchful and unable to let down, which meant he noticed triggers even faster. He finally came for help after realizing he was organizing his entire workday around how to avoid being caught off guard, yet still having flashback-like moments in class. What frightened him most was the possibility that this was simply who he was now: a man who could not protect himself, could not relax, and could not be fully present for the students who depended on him. What he hoped, cautiously, was that he might learn how to walk into a room without first looking for the exits and without feeling the parking lot come rushing back.
